simple: the part of the kernel that offers one set of file operations and passes each request to the right file system.
analogy: the front desk that sends each request slip to the right library.
precise: a kernel layer that defines file-system-independent objects (mounted file systems, vnodes or inodes, directory-entry caches, open files) and an operations interface each concrete file system implements; system calls such as open and read are written once against it.
source: D3, D1 of F3-31 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the kernel's record for one file or directory, the same shape whatever file system it lives on.
analogy: the desk's index card for a book, which names the library that holds it.
precise: an in-memory object representing one file-system object, holding its type, size, permissions and a pointer to an operations table supplied by its file system (Linux calls the equivalent object an inode; the name vnode comes from the BSD and SunOS tradition).
source: D3, D2 of F3-31 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: attaching one file system into the tree of another, at a directory.
analogy: a door from the main library into the science room's shelf.
precise: an entry in the kernel's mount table binding the root of a file system to a directory (the mount point) of an already mounted one; path lookup that reaches the mount point continues in the mounted root.
source: D3, D1 of F3-31 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the small number a program uses for an open file, and the kernel record behind it that remembers the current position.
analogy: a numbered ticket in your hand, and the desk's note of how far you have read.
precise: a per-process index into a descriptor table; each entry points to an open-file description holding the offset and access mode; dup and fork create descriptors that share one description and therefore one offset.
source: D4, D1 of F3-31 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a packed set of files that the boot loader puts into memory next to the kernel, so the kernel has files before it has disk drivers.
analogy: the box of books that arrives with the principal on the first day.
precise: an archive or file-system image loaded into memory by the boot loader (here as a Multiboot module) and mounted by the kernel, usually as its first root file system.
source: D5, C1 of F3-31 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a standard way of packing files one after another, each with a 512-byte label in front.
analogy: books packed in the box, each with a label card on top.
precise: the "ustar" interchange format of the POSIX pax utility: a sequence of 512-byte header blocks, each followed by the file's data padded to whole 512-byte blocks, ended by blocks of zeros.
source: D4 of F3-31 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a device you read and write in fixed-size pieces by number, like a disk.
analogy: the shelves, where books sit at numbered places.
precise: a device whose interface transfers whole blocks addressed by block number, with no notion of files; file systems are built on top of it.
source: D1 of F3-31 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: copies of recently used disk blocks kept in memory, so most reads and writes do not touch the disk.
analogy: the librarian's trolley of recently used books.
precise: a kernel cache of block-device blocks indexed by (device, block number), with a replacement policy such as least recently used and a write policy (write-through or write-back with a sync operation).
source: D2, D1 of F3-31 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: write-back saves a change to the disk later; write-through saves it at once.
analogy: notes added to the trolley copy now and taken to the shelves on the next trip, or carried to the shelves immediately.
precise: in write-through every write to a cached block is also written to the device before the operation completes; in write-back the cached block is marked dirty and written when it is evicted or when a sync is requested.
source: D2, D1 of F3-31 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: when the cache is full, throw out the block nobody has used for the longest time.
analogy: the book at the bottom of the trolley pile goes back to the shelf first.
precise: a replacement policy that evicts the entry whose last access is oldest, commonly kept as a list ordered by access time.
source: D1 of F3-31 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a simple, old and very widely understood way of storing files on a disk, with a big table that links the pieces of each file.
analogy: the old library with its ledger of "continued on shelf n" lines.
precise: the 32-bit-entry variant of Microsoft's File Allocation Table file system: a boot sector with a BIOS parameter block, reserved sectors including FSInfo, one or more copies of the FAT, and a data area of clusters, where directories are ordinary cluster chains of 32-byte entries.
source: D1 of F3-32 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a sector is the smallest piece the disk reads; a cluster is the piece of space the file system hands out, one or more sectors.
analogy: a page, and the folder of pages that fits one shelf.
precise: the sector is the device's addressing unit (512 bytes on the lab volume); a cluster is a run of 2n consecutive sectors in the data area, numbered from 2; file space is allocated in whole clusters.
source: D1 of F3-32 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: numbers at the start of the volume that describe its shape.
analogy: the plan of the library pinned at the entrance.
precise: fields in the boot sector (sector 0) giving bytes per sector, sectors per cluster, reserved sector count, number of FATs, total sectors, FAT size, the root directory's first cluster and the FSInfo sector, stored little-endian.
source: D1 of F3-32 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a table with one number per cluster saying which cluster comes next in the file, or that the cluster is free or the last one.
analogy: the ledger with one "continued on shelf n" line per shelf.
precise: an array indexed by cluster number; entry value 0 means free, a value ≥ 0x0FFFFFF8 means end of chain, other values give the next cluster; in FAT32 the top 4 bits of each 32-bit entry are reserved and must be preserved.
source: D1 of F3-32 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of clusters one file uses, linked through the FAT.
analogy: following "continued on" lines from the first shelf to "end".
precise: a linked list starting at the first cluster recorded in the directory entry and continuing through FAT entries until an end-of-chain mark.
source: D1 of F3-32 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a 32-byte record holding a file's short name, kind, dates, first cluster and size.
analogy: the old catalogue card with eight letters and a three-letter kind.
precise: a 32-byte structure in a directory's clusters: 11 bytes of name (8 base, 3 extension, space-padded, upper case), an attribute byte, timestamps, the high and low 16 bits of the first cluster, and a 32-bit size; first byte 0xE5 marks a deleted entry and 0x00 the end of the directory.
source: D1 of F3-32 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: extra 32-byte records directly in front of a short-name entry that hold the real, long name.
analogy: the extra title cards in front of the old card, each with a check number.
precise: a directory entry with attribute 0x0F holding 13 UCS-2 characters, a sequence number (0x40 set on the last part, which is stored first) and a checksum of the 11-byte short name it belongs to.
source: D1 of F3-32 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the "~1" in a short name like README~1.TXT, added so a long name gets a unique short form.
analogy: numbering two cards that would otherwise look the same.
precise: the suffix "~n" written into the last characters of the 8-character base of a generated short name, with the smallest n that makes the name unique in its directory.
source: D1 of F3-32 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a note on the volume that remembers how many clusters are free, so nobody has to count.
analogy: the "free shelves: 80,376" board at the entrance.
precise: a reserved sector, located by the BPB, with three signatures, a free-cluster count and a next-free hint; both values are hints that a driver may recompute (0xFFFFFFFF means unknown).
source: D1 of F3-32 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: space marked as used in the FAT that no file points to.
analogy: a shelf the ledger says is taken, but no card leads to it.
precise: a cluster (or chain) whose FAT entry is non-zero but which is not reachable from any directory entry; a checker such as fsck.fat reports it and can free it or save it as a file.
source: D3 of F3-32 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the "second extended file system", the classic Linux disk format, built from inodes, bitmaps and block groups.
analogy: the many-floored library with charts and record cards.
precise: a block-based file system whose volume is divided into block groups, each with a block bitmap, an inode bitmap and an inode table; files are inodes with block pointers, and directories map names to inode numbers.
source: D1, D2 of F3-33 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the block that describes the whole volume: its size, block size and how many things are free.
analogy: the plan at the entrance of the building.
precise: a 1024-byte structure at byte offset 1024 of the volume (with backup copies in some groups) holding counts, sizes, the magic number 0xEF53, feature flags and state.
source: D1 of F3-33 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a slice of the disk with its own maps and its own inodes, and the small record that says where those maps are.
analogy: one floor, with its own charts and drawer, and the floor directory at the entrance.
precise: a run of blocks_per_group consecutive blocks; the group descriptor table, in the block(s) after the superblock, gives each group's block-bitmap, inode-bitmap and inode-table locations and its free counts.
source: D1 of F3-33 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the record of one file: its type, permissions, size, times and where its blocks are, but not its name.
analogy: the record card in the drawer.
precise: a fixed-size entry in an inode table, addressed by inode number (counting from 1), with mode, owner, size, timestamps, link count and an array of 15 block pointers: 12 direct, one single-, one double- and one triple-indirect.
source: D1, D3 of F3-33 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a block that holds block numbers instead of file data, for files too large for the inode's own list.
analogy: the "list shelf" with a sheet of further shelf numbers.
precise: a block of 32-bit block numbers (block size / 4 of them); a single-indirect block maps data blocks, a double-indirect block maps single-indirect blocks, and so on.
source: D1 of F3-33 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a row of bits, one per block or inode, saying used (1) or free (0).
analogy: the shaded-square charts by the stairs.
precise: one block per group whose bit i records whether block (or inode) i of that group is allocated; the allocator searches them and the free counts in the group descriptor and superblock summarise them.
source: D1 of F3-33 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a record in a directory that links a name to an inode number.
analogy: a line in the catalogue: title → card number.
precise: a variable-length record with inode number, record length, name length, file type (with the filetype feature) and the name; record lengths chain the entries through each directory block, and deleting merges a record into its predecessor.
source: D1 of F3-33 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a second name for the same file, and the counter of how many names a file has.
analogy: two catalogue lines leading to one card.
precise: any directory entry naming an inode; the inode's i_links_count counts them (a directory counts its name, its own "." and every child's ".."), and the inode and its blocks are freed only when the count reaches 0 and no process has it open.
source: D3, D2 of F3-33 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a program that reads the whole file system and checks that all its records agree.
analogy: the head librarian comparing every card with the charts.
precise: the ext2/3/4 checker of e2fsprogs; in passes it checks inodes and their blocks, directory structure, connectivity, reference counts and group summaries against each other, and repairs or (with -n) only reports differences.
source: D4 of F3-33 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: making sure that a power cut in the middle of an update leaves the disk in a state that is still safe to use or easy to repair.
analogy: shelving in an order that leaves at worst a shaded square with no book, never two cards for one shelf.
precise: the property that every prefix of a file system's write sequence leaves a state from which the invariants can be restored without losing or exposing data, achieved by write ordering, journaling or copy-on-write.
source: D2 of F3-33 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: any way for separate programs to pass data or signals to each other.
analogy: the tubes, boards and bells between closed classrooms.
precise: the kernel mechanisms that let processes with separate address spaces exchange data or synchronise: pipes, shared memory, message queues, sockets, events and signals.
source: D1 of F3-34 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a one-way channel of bytes: one program writes at one end, another reads at the other.
analogy: the message tube between two classrooms.
precise: a kernel object holding a bounded byte buffer, with a read end and a write end exposed as file descriptors; reads block while it is empty and writes block while it is full, and closing all write ends gives readers end of file.
source: D2, D1 of F3-34 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of threads sleeping until something happens to an object.
analogy: pupils waiting at the tube for the bell.
precise: a kernel list of blocked threads attached to an object and a condition; the code that changes the condition wakes some or all of them, and each woken thread re-checks the condition under the object's lock.
source: D1 of F3-34 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: memory that two programs can both see, so a value one writes the other can read.
analogy: the whiteboard in the wall between two rooms.
precise: physical frames mapped into the page tables of two or more processes (possibly at different virtual addresses), created anonymously and inherited across fork, or named and opened by each process.
source: D2, D1 of F3-34 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a kernel flag that one thread sets and another waits for.
analogy: the bell.
precise: a waitable object with a signalled state; with auto-reset, one waiting thread is released and the event is cleared; with manual reset, all waiters are released and it stays signalled until reset.
source: D3 of F3-34 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a counter you can wait on: waiting takes one unit or sleeps until there is one; posting adds one.
analogy: a bowl of tokens by the door.
precise: a non-negative integer with atomic wait (decrement, blocking at zero) and post (increment, waking a waiter); a semaphore with values 0 and 1 used across processes behaves as an auto-reset event.
source: D1, D2 of F3-34 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one call that sleeps until any one of several things is ready.
analogy: a teacher waiting for whichever of three bells rings first.
precise: a primitive that blocks a thread on a set of waitable objects and returns which became signalled (Windows WaitForMultipleObjects; on POSIX, poll or select over file descriptors).
source: D3, D2 of F3-34 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a bug where a thread sleeps forever because the signal that should have woken it went to someone else or came before it slept.
analogy: only one of two waiting pupils hears the bell.
precise: a synchronisation failure in which a state change that allows a blocked thread to proceed does not wake it, because the wake-up was skipped, delivered to another thread, or raced with the decision to sleep.
source: D1 of F3-34 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small numbered notice the kernel delivers to a process, interrupting what it is doing.
analogy: a knock on the classroom door during a lesson.
precise: an asynchronous notification identified by a number (for example SIGPIPE, SIGINT), delivered by running a registered handler, ignoring it or taking a default action such as terminating the process.
source: D2 of F3-34 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: all the programs that run outside the kernel: shells, tools, libraries.
analogy: the pupils and helpers in the hall, outside the office.
precise: code running in the processor's unprivileged mode in process address spaces, reaching the kernel only through system calls.
source: D1 of F3-35 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a program that reads commands you type and runs other programs for you.
analogy: the receptionist who turns spoken requests into forms and helpers.
precise: a command interpreter that parses command lines, creates processes for commands, connects their standard input and output to files and pipes, and reports exit statuses; the POSIX shell language defines its grammar.
source: D2 of F3-35 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: several commands joined by |, each one's output feeding the next one's input.
analogy: helpers passing papers along a row.
precise: a sequence of commands run as concurrent processes, where the standard output of each is connected by a pipe to the standard input of the next; its exit status is the last command's.
source: D2 of F3-35 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: making a program read from or write to a file instead of the keyboard or screen.
analogy: telling a helper "take your papers from this folder".
precise: shell syntax (<, >, >>) that opens a file and installs it as descriptor 0 or 1 of the command with dup2 before exec.
source: D2 of F3-35 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a command the shell does itself instead of starting a program.
analogy: the receptionist moving her own desk.
precise: a command executed inside the shell process, required when it must change the shell's own state (current directory, exit, variables).
source: D2 of F3-35 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number a program gives back when it ends: 0 for success, other values for problems.
analogy: the tick or cross on the board.
precise: the value passed to exit, collected by the parent with waitpid; the shell stores the last one in $?, uses 127 for "command not found" and 128 + n for death by signal n.
source: D2 of F3-35 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the standard set of functions every C program can call, like printf and strlen, plus the code that talks to the kernel for them.
analogy: the school's standard forms.
precise: the implementation of the ISO C standard library (and usually POSIX interfaces), consisting of portable code, a system-call layer for one kernel and architecture, start-up code that calls main, and headers.
source: D3, D2 of F3-35 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the small part of a C library that knows how to ask one particular kernel for things.
analogy: the office-specific version of the forms.
precise: the functions that load system-call numbers and arguments into the registers a kernel and architecture expect, execute the trap instruction and convert results and errors; porting a library to a new OS means writing this layer.
source: D4 of F3-35 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the first code that runs in a program, before main.
analogy: the receptionist opening the folder and handing out the first page.
precise: the entry point the kernel jumps to; it reads the argument count, argument and environment pointers from the initial stack as the ABI defines, initialises the library and calls exit(main(argc, argv)).
source: D5 of F3-35 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: collecting output in memory and writing it in bigger pieces.
analogy: collecting slips and taking them to the office in one trip.
precise: the C library's stdio buffer for each stream, flushed when full, at a newline (line-buffered, the usual mode for terminals), or only when full or at exit (fully buffered, the usual mode for files and pipes).
source: D3 of F3-35 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a saved, known-correct record of a session that a new run must match exactly.
analogy: the answer sheet for the practical exam.
precise: an expected output file, produced independently of the system under test, compared byte for byte with the captured output of a scripted session.
source: C1 of F3-35 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)
